title: Security Operations and Threat Mitigation

sources.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Contingency Planning Guide
sources.scope: Read Executive Summary and Ch. 1-2 (PDF pp. 13-26): plan distinctions, contingency process, BCP/DRP, resilience. Also inspected Ch. 3 TOC; detailed RTO/RPO passages not separately retrieved.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Firewall Guidelines
sources.scope: Read PDF pp. 1-18: firewall policy, packet filtering, stateful inspection, application firewalls, proxy and WAF overview; allowed traffic, specific rules, testing and management.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-128 Security-Focused Configuration Management
sources.scope: Read PDF pp. 48-53, Sec. 3.3: access restrictions, requested/evaluated/tested/approved changes, verify deployment, emergency change, impact analysis, retain old baseline for rollback.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Authentication and Authenticator Management
sources.scope: Read normative password and authenticator requirements, Sec. 3.1.1 and AAL summary: 15-character single-factor and 8-character MFA-only minimums, blocklist, composition, manager, rate limiting.

sources.title: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3
sources.scope: Read Sections 1-2: secure-channel goals, handshake negotiation and authentication, record protection, and weaker replay/forward-secrecy properties of 0-RTT.

sources.title: RFC 4251 SSH Protocol Architecture
sources.scope: Read Sections 1, 4.1, 4.4 and 9: SSH transport properties, host-key verification, client authentication, and configuration policy.

sources.title: RFC 5280 X.509 Certificate and CRL Profile
sources.scope: Read Sections 3.1-3.3: CA-signed key-to-subject binding, certification paths, trust, CRLs and revocation limits.

sources.title: NIST SP 1800-16 TLS Server Certificate Management
sources.scope: Read certificate background and issuance process: server identity, key-pair CSR, RA review, CA issuance, chain validation, expiry, private-key risks.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-94 IDPS Guide
sources.scope: Read Executive Summary and Ch. 2: IDS/IPS purposes and signature, anomaly, and stateful protocol detection methodologies. Document dates from 2007; platform-neutral concepts only.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-115 Technical Guide to Security Testing
sources.scope: Read Executive Summary, Ch. 1-2, and targeted Ch. 5-7 passages: assessment planning, risk, scope, execution/data handling, pen-test phases/logistics, reporting, and ROE appendix identified in TOC.

sources.title: NIST CSRC Glossary: Masking
sources.scope: Read definition: removing/replacing a field in a way that does not preserve analytic utility; examples include asterisks or random pseudonyms.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-188 De-Identifying Government Datasets
sources.scope: Read summary of de-identification goals, risk evaluation, removing identifiers, transforming quasi-identifiers, synthetic data, and warning that simple masking may not suffice.

sources.title: CISA et al. Phishing Guidance: Phase One
sources.scope: Read pp. 3-12: phishing definitions, email/link/attachment lures, filtering, least privilege, patching, training, incident response, and reporting.

sources.title: CISA Use Strong Passwords
sources.scope: Read guidance on unique passwords, password managers, long/random passwords, and MFA.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Controls Catalog
sources.scope: Read publication overview and control families. Catalog scope supports governance context; no individual control text claimed.

sources.title: SplashKit Steganography Guide
sources.scope: Read guide explaining carrier media and image LSB embedding; explicitly distinguishes hiding message existence from encryption and says combine with encryption for sensitive content.

pages.title: Policies and recovery plans
notes: AUP states permitted use of organizational systems.
InfoSec policy sets security duties and requirements.
Policy sets what; procedures describe how to do it.
BCP sustains priority business processes through disruption.
DRP restores systems and data after a disaster.
DRP supports BCP; neither plan is itself a backup.
BIA ranks processes, systems, and dependency priorities.
Preventive controls reduce likelihood or disruption impact.
Plans name activation triggers, teams, contacts, and roles.

pages.title: Recovery targets and exercise
notes: RTO is the target time to restore a service.
RPO is the acceptable age of restored data.
RTO limits outage duration; RPO limits data loss.
Recovery strategy follows impact and criticality analysis.
Define recovery sequence, resources, locations, and contacts.
Test, train, and exercise; testing validates recovery ability.
Tabletops test decisions; restores test usable recovered data.
Compare actual restore time and data age with targets.
Record gaps, corrective owners, and retest evidence.
Update plans when systems, risks, or roles change.

pages.title: Secure messaging and email
notes: Verify recipients and addresses before sending sensitive data.
Use approved protected channels for sensitive communications.
TLS protects a connection; it does not protect every copy.
HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS, not a separate cipher.
Certificate validation helps authenticate the server endpoint.
Email encryption depends on keys and recipient configuration.
Unexpected urgency, links, or files can signal phishing.
Verify unusual payment requests on a separate known channel.
Report suspicious messages through approved response channels.

pages.title: Data minimization and change control
notes: Collect only data needed for a defined business purpose.
Less stored data reduces exposure after unauthorized access.
Classify data; follow access, retention, and disposal rules.
Share only necessary fields with authorized recipients.
Masking replaces or removes fields, reducing analytic utility.
Masked data can still identify via other attributes.
Tokens substitute values; secure any identity mapping.
Change requests need recording and security impact review.
Test and approve changes before deployment; then verify them.
Archive prior baselines for traceability and rollback.

practice.prompt: A restore finishes in 9 hours with a 6-hour RTO. What follows?
practice.answer: The restore test missed the recovery-time target. Identify bottlenecks and dependencies, assign improvement work, then retest; successful backup completion alone does not establish recovery capability.

practice.prompt: Why verify recipients even when email uses encryption?
practice.answer: Encryption can protect a channel or message contents, but it cannot prevent disclosure to an incorrectly selected recipient or remove unnecessary data already sent.

pages.title: Firewall inspection models
notes: A firewall controls flows across different security postures.
Network firewall filters traffic crossing network boundaries.
Host firewall filters traffic to and from its endpoint.
Stateless filter checks each packet without session tracking.
Fields include addresses, protocol, ports, and direction.
Stateful inspection tracks flows in a connection state table.
Stateful filters compare packets with expected session state.
Return traffic may pass when linked to an allowed session.
State tracking does not inspect all application meaning.

pages.title: NGFW, WAF, and limits
notes: Application firewall inspects protocol content and behavior.
NGFW commonly combines network controls and added inspection.
NGFW capabilities differ across vendors and configurations.
WAF focuses on HTTP requests to web applications.
WAF can filter web-specific inputs and request patterns.
WAF supplements; it does not replace network firewalls.
Encrypted traffic can limit inspection without termination.
NAT translates addresses; translation alone is not a firewall.
Firewalls cannot stop every attack or internal misuse.
Use endpoint, identity, and monitoring controls in depth.

pages.title: ACL rules and least privilege
notes: ACL is an ordered set of permit and deny conditions.
Rules match source, destination, protocol, port, direction.
Permit only traffic required by documented business need.
Narrow addresses and services rather than broad any-any rules.
Rule order matters when the first matching rule decides.
Default-deny blocks traffic not explicitly permitted.
Apply policy to both inbound and outbound flows.
Use logs and alerts to observe rule effects and threats.
Review stale rules and exceptions through change control.

pages.title: Segmentation, tests, and operation
notes: Separate public web, application, and data trust zones.
Allow web tier to reach only required database service.
Block direct public access to internal database systems.
Restrict administration to approved hosts and accounts.
Test permitted flows and expected denials before rollout.
Deploy changes in stages and monitor service impact.
Rollback plan reduces outage risk from incorrect rules.
Broad rules permit excess access and lateral movement.
Overly strict rules can block legitimate business traffic.
Review rules periodically and after topology changes.

practice.prompt: A database needs web-tier access only. What rule is narrow?
practice.answer: Permit the web-tier source to the required database service, and deny other routes under policy. This follows least privilege and avoids public any-to-any exposure.

practice.prompt: How do stateless and stateful inspection differ?
practice.answer: Stateless filtering evaluates each packet's fields without tracking a flow; stateful inspection keeps connection state and checks packets against it. Stateful behavior has resource and routing assumptions.

sheets.title: Secure Protocols, Detection, and Data Methods

pages.title: SSH, HTTPS, TLS, and WPA2
notes: SSH supports secure remote login over an insecure network.
SSH authenticates its server and protects data integrity.
Verify SSH host keys to detect server impersonation.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS; TLS is the security protocol.
TLS handshake negotiates keys and protocol parameters.
TLS server identity is checked against its certificate.
TLS record layer protects application data in transit.
WPA2 protects a wireless link; use secure configuration.
Secure protocol use does not secure a compromised endpoint.

pages.title: Certificates and trust
notes: Certificate binds a public key to a named subject.
A trusted CA signs the binding under its issuance policy.
A chain links the server certificate to a trusted root key.
Client validates signatures, name, validity, and intended use.
Trust depends on local trust anchors and validation policy.
A certificate does not guarantee benign site content.
CA issues certificate after request and identity checks.
Keep the matching private key secret and access restricted.
Track expiry; expired certificates may break service.
CRLs list revoked certificates; updates introduce time lag.

pages.title: IDS and IPS mechanisms
notes: IDS monitors events and analyzes them for possible incidents.
IPS detects and attempts to stop possible incidents.
An IPS can block traffic or change a security control.
Signature detection compares events with known patterns.
Anomaly detection compares activity with expected behavior.
Stateful analysis checks protocol activity against profiles.
False positives report benign events as suspicious.
False negatives fail to detect a real incident.
Tune detections and validate alerts using event context.

pages.title: Malware, phishing, and data transformation
notes: Filter risky links and attachments at email gateways.
Least privilege limits malware damage after execution.
Check unexpected sender, destination, and request context.
Report suspicious email; avoid opening unexpected attachments.
Tokenization substitutes a token for a sensitive value.
Token mapping, if retained, needs separate access protection.
Masking removes or replaces fields and can lose analytic use.
Steganography conceals a message within a carrier medium.
Steganography hides presence; it is not encryption.
Obfuscation is not encryption; each method has limits.

practice.prompt: A TLS certificate is valid. Does that prove a site is safe?
practice.answer: No. Validation helps authenticate a server name and public key through a trust chain, but it does not certify that the site's content or actions are harmless.

practice.prompt: An IPS blocks an unusual but valid request. What issue may exist?
practice.answer: It may be a false positive or unsuitable rule. Review the event and detection context, tune controls carefully, and assess service impact before changing prevention policy.

sheets.title: Password Security, Patching, and Authorized Testing

pages.title: Current password requirements
notes: NIST minimum is 15 characters for single-factor passwords.
MFA-only password minimum is 8 characters under NIST.
Use the correct context; 15 is not universal to MFA.
NIST rejects extra composition rules for these passwords.
Block commonly used, expected, and compromised passwords.
Allow password managers, autofill, and paste functionality.
Rate limiting helps reduce online guessing attempts.
Do not require arbitrary periodic changes absent compromise.
Change passwords promptly when compromise evidence exists.

pages.title: Password use and protection
notes: Use a unique password for each account or service.
Long unique secrets reduce reuse and guessing risks.
A manager can generate and store distinct passwords.
MFA adds a separate factor beyond the password.
Password plus another password is not two factor types.
Passwords alone are not phishing-resistant authentication.
NIST recommends blocklisting weak or breached candidates.
Verifiers hash passwords with salt and high work factor.
A salt is not secret; it prevents identical hash reuse.
Account recovery needs protection too.

pages.title: Patches and secure change
notes: Updates repair flaws and may change software behavior.
Inventory systems to identify exposed, affected versions.
Prioritize patches by risk, exposure, and business impact.
Obtain updates through authenticated vendor distribution.
Test security and function before production deployment.
Approve changes after security-impact assessment and testing.
Verify deployment and update affected system documentation.
Emergency changes still need later documented review.
Patch firewall software to address vendor security flaws.

pages.title: Version control and pen testing
notes: Version control tracks change history and prior baselines.
Review diffs to find unexpected or unsafe configuration edits.
Keep passwords, tokens, keys, and private data out of commits.
Retain prior known-good versions for tested rollback.
Pen testing validates weaknesses under agreed conditions.
Obtain explicit written authorization before any testing.
Scope lists targets, exclusions, dates, and permitted methods.
Rules of engagement set contacts and stop conditions.
Protect evidence; report findings for remediation and retest.
Out-of-scope discovery means stop and contact the owner.

practice.prompt: Which password minimum applies: single factor or MFA-only?
practice.answer: NIST SP 800-63B-4 sets 15 characters for single-factor use and 8 when used only as part of MFA. Identify the context before selecting the minimum; do not apply one value to both.

practice.prompt: A tester sees an admin host outside written scope. What next?
practice.answer: Stop activity on that host and notify the named contact under the rules of engagement. Authorization is limited to the documented scope; curiosity does not extend permission.

lab.title: Fictional incident and change tabletop
steps: Use only imaginary service, account, and network details.
Sort a suspicious email into verify, report, or safely discard.
Review a sample change request and a short configuration diff.
Map one allowed web-to-data flow and one blocked public flow.
Read a fictional pen-test scope and judge an out-of-scope finding.
expected: Learner does not open the suspicious file and reports it.
Change request includes impact review, approval, test, and rollback.
ACL allows only the necessary application flow.
Testing stops at the scope boundary and owner is notified.
